result.topic_en: Latin draft from the heat-conduction prize memoir: for the equation Λu = ∂u/∂t, it treats exponential solutions f(t)e^{λt} and the cases where λ is real or complex. It shows how the auxiliary equation Δu = 0 restricts the form of the solution u.

$\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial x_1} = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial x_2} = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial x_3} = 0$ sive $\alpha = $ const., quum forma $(a_{\iota,\iota'}\quad)$ ut

2°. Quando $\lambda$ est formae $\mu+\nu i$ et $\mu,\nu$ sunt functiones independentes ipsarum
$x_1, x_2, x_3$, quantitates $\mu+\nu i$ et $\mu-\nu i$ pro variabilibus independentibus
$\alpha$ et $\beta$ sumi poterunt, continebitque ipsum $u$ praeter terminum $f(t)e^{\alpha t}$
etiam terminum complexum conjugatum $\varphi(t)e^{\beta t}$. Quodsi
$\Delta u = a\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial\alpha^2} + b\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial\alpha\partial\beta} + c\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial\beta^2} + e\frac{\partial u}{\partial\alpha} + f\frac{\partial u}{\partial\beta}$
est, ex aequatione $\Delta u = 0$ substituendo $u = f(t)e^{\alpha t}$ et aequando coefficientem ipsius $t^{n}e^{\alpha t}$ cifrae, obtinetur $a = 0$, et perinde $b = 0$ ($c = 0$)
substituendo $u = \varphi(t)e^{\beta t}$. Unde ope aequationis $\Delta u = 0$ aequatio $\Lambda u = \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}$
ita transformari potest, ut solos quotientes differentiales secundum alteram utram variabilem contineat. Sed substituendo $u = f(t)e^{\alpha t}$, $u =$
$\varphi(t)e^{\beta t}$ coefficiens summi cujusque horum quotientium differentialium
invenitur $= 0$, unde et hi quotientes differentiales ex aequatione
$\Lambda u = \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}$ omnes excidere debent, q. e. d.

In casu igitur posteriore functio $u$ componitur e numero finito
terminorum formae $f(t)e^{\lambda t}$, in quibus $\lambda$ est constans et $f(t)$ functio
integra ipsius $t$.
In casu priore quando habetur aequatio formae
(1) $\sum_\nu a_\nu \frac{\partial^\nu u}{\partial\alpha^\nu} = 0$
functio $u$ erit formae
$u = \sum_\nu q_\nu p_\nu$
denotantibus $p_1, p_2 \ldots$ solutiones particulares aequationis (1) et $q_1, q_2 \ldots$
constantes arbitrarias sive functiones solarum $\beta$ et $t$. Quodsi haec expressio in aequatione
$\Lambda u = \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}$
substituitur, obtinetur aequatio formae
$\sum PQ = 0$
in qua quantitates $Q$ sunt quotientes differentiales ipsarum $q$ ideoque
functiones solarum $\beta$ et $t$, quantitates $P$ autem functiones solarum $\alpha$ et $\beta$.

methods.what: Substituting the exponential terms into a general second-order operator Δu and equating to zero the coefficient of t^n e^{αt} forces its second-order coefficients to vanish
methods.quote: ex aequatione $\Delta u = 0$ substituendo $u = f(t)e^{\alpha t}$ et aequando coefficientem ipsius $t^{n}e^{\alpha t}$ cifrae, obtinetur $a = 0$, et perinde $b = 0$ ($c = 0$)

methods.what: Conclusion of the complex case: u is a finite sum of terms f(t)e^{λt}, with λ constant and f a polynomial (entire function) in t
methods.quote:
functio $u$ componitur e numero finito

integra ipsius $t$

methods.what: In the real case, u is written as a sum of particular solutions p_ν of an ordinary differential equation in α, with coefficients q_ν depending only on β and t; substituting gives ΣPQ = 0
